The chromatic trumpet is a brass instrument, Hornbostel-Sachs number 423.233, and the source gives its culture area as the Middle East / the Mediterranean. The modern trumpet is mostly made of brass tubing, bent twice into a rounded rectangle; the player vibrates the lips in the mouthpiece, which sets up a standing wave in the air column inside and makes the sound. The instrument usually has three, occasionally four, pistons or rotary valves, and pressing a valve adds length to the tubing and lowers the pitch, so the trumpet can play a full chromatic scale. It is played by trumpeters, and is common in orchestras, wind bands, chamber music, jazz ensembles, popular music and school bands.

Its timbre is mainly bright, and the C trumpet is brighter still because its tube is shorter; the piccolo trumpet reaches one of the highest ranges in the brass family, while the bass trumpet sounds an octave below the standard B flat instrument. The player changes pitch, volume and timbre with the lips and the amount of breath, and three or four valves change the length of the tube so that a full chromatic scale is available. Compared with the cornet, the trumpet has a cylindrical bore, the cornet a conical one.

Early horns were of bronze, silver, metal, bone and ram's horn: the bronze and silver trumpets from Tutankhamun's tomb, the salpinx of bone or bronze, the shofar of ram's horn, and a trumpet of the Bactria-Margiana culture in Central Asia made from a single sheet of metal. The word trump, meaning a trumpet, is first recorded in English in 1300. It comes from Old French and means a long tubular instrument (about the eleventh century), and is related to Provençal and Italian words, which may come from Germanic (compare the Old High German and Old Norse words for trumpet), with an onomatopoeic origin. According to historical records, around 1940 a band of three trumpeters performed in Toledo, Ohio, in the United States. As an instrument, the trumpet's changing name reflects the cultural exchange and the spread of music between the languages of medieval Europe.
